terms.grammar: verb, fourth conjugation, deponent, with the dative
evidence: Cic. de Or. 1.126: valdē tibi adsentior
terms.comment: Often printed adsentior. Assentior on its own is “I agree”. The active assentiō is rare: Plautus, Vergil, and three times in Cicero’s letters (Lewis & Short).

terms.gloss: agree, be of one mind (cum aliquō, dē rē)
evidence: Cic. Lael. 86: dē amīcitiae ūtilitāte omnēs ūnō ōre cōnsentiunt (Lewis & Short)
Cic. Tusc. 1.35: omnium cōnsēnsus nātūrae vōx est (Lewis & Short)
Caes. BG 1.30: ex commūnī cōnsēnsū (Lewis & Short)
Cic. de Or. 1.5: solēsque nōn numquam hāc dē rē ā mē in disputātiōnibus nostrīs dissentīre

phrases.latin: illud vērō quod ā tē dictum est … valdē tibi adsentior
phrases.english: but what you said … I entirely agree with

phrases.latin: Dē eā rē tēcum funditus cōnsentiō.
phrases.english: I agree with you completely on that point.

sources: Lewis & Short: assentior · Lewis & Short: consentio · Lewis & Short: dissentio · Lewis & Short: consensus
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, pp. 96, 148, 177, 270.
Quotations of Cicero’s De oratore (Wilkins) that are not in the loci collections were checked against the Perseus Latin texts (9 November 2026).
Quotations marked “Lewis & Short” are given as Lewis & Short cites them, with its references, in the house spelling (macrons, consonantal j); they have not been checked against a modern edition.
